items.title: Welcome!
items.text: I made this site to catalog the various resources for COMP3991. Where possible I will provide some explanations for the concepts but note that I may still be trying to wrap my head around them myself :D.

items.title: Preface
items.text:
This is the first time the course is being run, as such we really have no prior testing material to go off of with regards to questions. The course is heavily based on Mike Cohen's work on Calculus and Linear Algebra so we may assume that the examinations will be similar to his exercises. Dr. Manohar really like proofs however so although it's an "Applied Math" course you should expect quite a few proofs.

For this guide I will be speaking from my own experience with math and will be showing my approach to this course. You do not need to follow my approach, however I hope the resources are helpful. If you have any additional resources you wish to share with the class, feel free to send them to me and I will update the page.

items.title: My Approach
items.text:
Math is a very tricky subject, most people (me included) can’t just sit down and listen to math be explained. The key is repetition. When learning math I use an approach called the blackbox method. The short of that is this: “You do not need to understand how something works to use it.”

I tend to approach topics in math by solving the questions first then understanding why the method works later when I have more experience with it. The proof based approach taken in class is the opposite, we learn why things work before we use them.

The issue I have with this approach is that it overwhelms the listener with information. Proofs by their nature are very verbose and they describe things that the listener may have no experience at all working with.

We're mostly lucky in that this course is an applied math course so every concept we learn has a physical (or digital) impact that it can be related to. This greatly helps in forming that intuition for problem solving.

My advice, keep practicing questions, look at solutions, build a connection with the tools then try to understand them.

items.title: Differentiation Basics
items.text: This is where I'd recommend you start if you don't understand differentiation. The video is quite long but it covers nearly everything we need to know under differentiation, you can skip through the chapters to any struggle points.

items.title: Differentiation from First Principles
items.text: First principles is the definition of the derivative, it's basically the proof for why differentiation works. It's included in the video above but I put it here as well since we're going to need it for the proofs.

items.title: Differentiation Formulae
items.text:
When we're finding the derivative of a function, it is almost never going to be in the simple form f(x). Because of this we need to know what to do when things break away from the norm like f(x)/g(x) or f(x)g(x). This material is also covered in the basics video but I added it here because we need to be able to prove them...

Note: He uses u and v in the video to teach the formulae, these just act as stand-ins for functions.

items.title: Limits
items.text: The Organic Chem Tutor is THE GOAT of math tutors, I highly recommend all of his videos for the Calculus topics covered thus far. If there's something he hasn't covered or you just don't like his style Khan Academy is another excellent resource!

items.title: Introduction to Limits
items.text: This video goes over the limits calculations in detail with explanations for continuity.

items.title: Limit of sin(x)/x
items.text: The course outline particularly calls attention to the limit of sin(x)/x as x tends to 0.
